speaker_role: Yale alumnus (2020 grad) who does paid interview coaching
commercial_incentive: Yes - offers paid 1:1 interview practice sessions via a booking link mentioned at the end
key_insights: For 'tell me about yourself,' speaker recommends talking 2-5 minutes since it acts as a launch pad prompting interviewer follow-up questions
Recommends using a 'lead' technique: mention an intriguing activity briefly without full detail so the interviewer asks a follow-up, creating a natural storytelling opening
Stories told in response should hit some combination of five themes: intellectual curiosity, selflessness/service, persistence/determination, and personal growth
For 'why this school,' pair a specific academic detail (a professor, program, or fellowship) with a personal/social or cultural connection to the school, avoiding generic praise
For social/community questions, answer with a specific concrete anecdote rather than abstract trait claims like 'I am loyal and kind'
Never answer 'no' when asked if you have questions for the interviewer; asking about the interviewer's favorite and least favorite experience is suggested as a good opener
Recommends heavy rehearsal: record yourself on camera and do many practice run-throughs, since over 50% of communication is described as non-verbal
Recommends sending a thank-you note after the interview and attaching a resume, since interviewers write up their notes shortly after and a resume can jog their memory
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker states more than 50% of communication is non-verbal (no source cited)
Speaker is self-identified as a Yale 2020 graduate
notable_or_distinctive: The 'lead' storytelling technique for interviews (deliberately under-explaining an activity to prompt a follow-up question) is a specific, non-generic tactic beyond typical 'be yourself' interview advice.
reliability_notes: Advice reflects one alum's personal interviewing philosophy, not documented admissions-office guidance; ends with a pitch for the speaker's paid coaching service; the 50%-nonverbal statistic is an unsourced commonly-repeated claim.
